Four candidates do it: Andre Lindqvist at $14,012,730 clears by $5,667,096, Amari Nakamura at $20,956,546 by $12,610,912, Alperen Vasquez at $25,118,979 by $16,773,345, and Andre Ferreira at $27,126,974 by $18,781,340. Lindqvist is the cheapest exit on the court, but $5,667,096 of surplus means you can absorb almost nothing in return, and a clean dump like that usually costs draft compensation. Nakamura's $12,610,912 of cushion is the sweet spot, since it lets you take back a smaller contract and still land under, which makes him materially easier to move than Lindqvist despite the bigger name. Do it before the season ends rather than at the deadline, because the second-apron penalties attach to where you finish.

**Verdict: LEGAL.** Cam Amadi at $3,362,774 clears, though only just. Memphis is at $217,547,563 with $4,138,437 of space beneath the second-apron hard cap of $221,686,000; the signing takes you to $220,910,337 and leaves $775,663. That $775,663 is your entire budget for the rest of the league year, under a ceiling you're forbidden to cross for any reason, injury replacements included. You'd also be at 15 players afterward, so the roster is effectively closed alongside the money. My recommendation depends on what Amadi is: if he's the guy, sign him and accept that the book shuts today. If he's depth, hold the space, because $4,138,437 buys a meaningfully better February option than $775,663 does, and this is the last moment you get to choose.

Everything except the room exception, which is the one you'd only want if you were operating with cap space in the first place. Brooklyn's apron salary is $150,832,379, under the tax line, so the full non-taxpayer mid-level of $12,822,000 is live, the taxpayer mid-level of $5,168,000 is live, the bi-annual is live, and minimum contracts are always there. One caveat on the bi-annual: the published amount for this season isn't in my table, so confirm that figure before you build an offer around it. The real decision isn't availability, it's hard caps. Using the non-taxpayer mid-level hard-caps you at the first apron of $178,132,000, the taxpayer version at the second apron of $188,931,000, the bi-annual also at the first apron, and minimums at nothing. Given how far your payroll sits from either line, that first-apron hard cap costs you essentially nothing in practice, so I'd default to the full $12,822,000 and treat the bi-annual as the second bite, rather than downgrading to the taxpayer mid-level to protect a ceiling you have no realistic path to reaching.

Start with the status that drives everything: an apron salary of $157,940,537, comfortably below the tax line, which keeps the whole toolbox open. The non-taxpayer mid-level of $12,822,000 is your largest weapon and the only genuine decision on the board, because spending any part of it hard-caps you at the first apron of $178,132,000 for the season. The taxpayer mid-level of $5,168,000 is technically available too, with a softer hard cap at the second apron of $188,931,000, but taking the smaller exception to preserve a ceiling that far above your payroll trades something real for something you'll never touch. The bi-annual exception is also in hand, though the published amount for this season isn't on file for me, so get that number confirmed before you shape an offer around it. Minimum deals round out the list with no hard cap at any payroll level, and the room exception is the only thing genuinely closed, since it exists solely for teams that renounce their exceptions and operate under the cap. With 13 players signed you have both the money and the roster spots to use two of these this summer.

By tax standards this is a modest bill: $11,380,912. Tax salary of $210,745,530 against the $200,428,000 line leaves $10,317,530 of overage, and it only reaches into the second bracket, with the first $6,064,000 taxed at 1x for $6,064,000 and the remaining $4,253,530 at 1.25x for $5,316,912. That's the cheap end of the curve, and the thing to understand is how fast it stops being cheap: rates climb by half a dollar per bracket from here, so the next slice of payroll you add costs substantially more than the one you just added. There's a second cost that never shows on the invoice, which is your forfeited share of the pool distributed to non-taxpaying teams, and it swings the true economics of ducking under the line. Since $10,317,530 is a single-contract problem at this payroll, it's worth pricing that trade out. The full swing is larger than the $11,380,912 headline once the distribution you'd recover is counted.

One contract does it; you don't need a multi-team construction. Washington's apron salary is $202,995,051 against a second apron of $188,931,000, so the gap is $14,064,051, and because you're already above that line you can neither aggregate salaries nor include cash in any deal. That forces a single-contract solution, and four names qualify: Isaiah Amadi at $28,051,930 clears the gap by $13,987,879, Terrance Sabonis at $29,377,764 by $15,313,713, Jaylen Osei at $38,341,955 by $24,277,904, and Bogdan Rees at $48,315,308 by $34,251,257, each assuming nothing comes back. Amadi at $13,987,879 of surplus is the cleanest basketball answer, keeping your rotation most intact. Rees at $34,251,257 is the one that also solves next season, since he's on an expiring deal and represents the largest number on the sheet. The thing to build into your ask: with no cash allowed, you're paying the other team in draft capital rather than dollars, so settle now on what a second-rounder is worth to ownership relative to the second-apron penalties you're buying your way out of.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** The signing misses by $1,158,950. Portland sits at $204,354,364, which leaves $4,660,636 beneath the first-apron hard cap of $209,015,000, and Amari Amadi at $5,819,586 would take you to $210,173,950, past a ceiling that allows no exceptions, no proration and no waivers. A hard cap isn't the apron; there's no penalty you can pay to cross it, the transaction simply won't be approved. If you want Amadi, either the number comes down to fit inside $4,660,636 or salary goes out first, and with 14 players on the roster you do have the spot, so this is purely a dollars problem rather than a roster one. Worth revisiting whether whatever triggered that hard cap was worth it, because that earlier decision is what's costing you this player.

Not over the second apron, and not close to it. Apron salary of $175,579,263 against a $188,931,000 second apron leaves $13,351,737 of room. The tighter line is the first apron: only $2,552,737 separates you from $178,132,000, and that's the threshold that would actually restrict what you can do. Note the composition as well, because it changes which number governs what. Salary and likely incentives come to $174,579,263, with $1,000,000 of unlikely incentives on Brennan Boateng, Kobe Sabonis and Dante Kearns counting toward the apron but not toward the tax, so you're $4,765,263 above the $170,814,000 tax line measured off the lower figure while your apron room is measured off the higher one. With 13 players and $2,552,737 of first-apron room, the roster spots you still have to fill will absorb most of that space, so if you intend to use anything bigger than a minimum contract, work out the sequencing before you make an offer.
